cards.explanation: The answer is trimmed his mustache, friends. Verse 24 says Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson, had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned safely. I know a thing or two about a mustache nobody manages, because mine has a mind of its own and it's also my hands. So he shows up to meet the king looking like he skipped every one of those.
The answer is “Why did you not go with me.” David asks, “Mephibosheth, why did you not go with me?” It's short and it goes straight at the point, friends. Mephibosheth has a lot to say in reply.

The answer is donkey, friends! No chariot, no fancy ride, just a donkey and a plan. Mephibosheth says, “I will have my donkey saddled so that I may ride on it and go with the king.” He says it right after he tells David he is lame (2 Samuel 19:26). Saddle up, ride along. I've had less clear plans than that, and I made mine in a junk drawer.

The answer is False, and Mephibosheth says it plainly. He tells David, “But my servant Ziba deceived me, and he has slandered your servant to my lord the king.” So he says Ziba deceived him and slandered him. That's the story he puts in front of the king.

The answer is that he asks the king to do what is good in his eyes. Mephibosheth says, “Yet my lord the king is like the angel of God, so do what is good in your eyes.” He doesn't hand David a list of demands, friends. He puts the decision in the king's hands.

The answer is table. Mephibosheth says the king set him “…among those who eat at your table.” David had told him he would always eat at his table (2 Samuel 9:7). So he's reminding the king of a seat he was already given.
The answer is divide, friends. David says, “I hereby declare that you and Ziba are to divide the land.” That's David's decision about the two men and the land. Mephibosheth answers it right away.

The answer is that he says, let Ziba take it all. Mephibosheth says, “Instead, since my lord the king has safely come to his own house, let Ziba take it all!” The text ties his words to the king getting home safely. I think that says a lot about what mattered to him.

The answer is True. The text says that since Barzillai was a very wealthy man, he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim. So when the king needed help there, Barzillai had it covered, friends. Barzillai the Gileadite was a man the king could count on.

The answer is Jerusalem, friends. David says, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you at my side in Jerusalem.” Barzillai had provided for the king, and now the king offers to provide for him. That's the offer on the table.

The answer is an added burden. Barzillai asks, “Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king?” The text says he had provided for the king while he stayed in Mahanaim (2 Samuel 19:32). I think he doesn't want to weigh David down.

The answer is True, friends. Barzillai says, “Your servant will go with the king only a short distance past the Jordan…” So he goes with David a short distance past the river, and no farther. He says so himself.

The answer is to die in his own city near his parents' tomb. Barzillai says, “Please let your servant return, that I may die in my own city near the tomb of my father and mother.” He asks for a spot near his parents' tomb, friends. I think it's a quiet, honest thing to ask.

The answer is that he asks the king to take Chimham across and do him good. Barzillai says, “Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him what is good in your sight.” Chimham is the man he puts forward to cross over with the king. Barzillai himself asks to return home, and the text says he did.

The answer is False, friends. David says, “Chimham will cross over with me, and I will do for him what is good in your sight…” Then he adds that he will do for Barzillai whatever he desires. It's a yes, and then some.

The answer is that David kisses him and blesses him. The text says, “The king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home.” A kiss and a blessing, and then he goes home, friends. That's a warm goodbye.

The answer is half, friends. The text says, “All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel escorted the king.” So Judah came in full, and Israel only half. Hold on to that, because it matters in the next verses.

The answer is that Judah took the king across secretly. The men of Israel ask, “Why did our brothers, the men of Judah, take you away secretly and bring the king and his household across the Jordan, together with all of David’s men?” They name Judah, their brothers, and they name the secret crossing. I think you can hear that they feel left out in how they ask.

The answer is that the king is their relative, friends. The men of Judah answer, “We did this because the king is our relative.” Then they ask why that angers Israel. It's a short answer, and they give it plainly.

The answer is False. The men of Judah ask, “Have we ever eaten at the king’s expense or received anything for ourselves?” They ask it as a question, friends, and I think the answer they want is no. They're saying they haven't taken a thing.

The answer is that they were the first to speak of restoring the king. The men of Israel say, “Were we not the first to speak of restoring our king?” They're saying they spoke up first, friends. It's one more reason they think they deserve a say.

The answer is True. The text says, “But the men of Judah spoke more fiercely than the men of Israel.” Israel made their case, and Judah's words came back fiercer, friends. That's how the passage ends.
